question: What is the primary purpose of disease surveillance in public health?

options.A: Continuous collection and analysis of health data
options.C: Providing direct bedside treatment to hospitalized patients
options.D: Enforcing hospital administrative policies and budgets

explanation: Surveillance is fundamentally an information-gathering and analytical activity used to guide public health decisions rather than direct clinical care. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h1)

question: Why is disease surveillance compared to an early warning radar system?

options.A: It measures the exact atmospheric pressure during epidemic seasons
options.B: It automatically sounds an audible alarm inside every primary health center
options.C: It detects potential health threats before they escalate into major crises
options.D: It uses satellite technology to track the geographic movement of patients

explanation: Just as radar spots incoming dangers early, surveillance systems track data trends to spot outbreaks before they overwhelm communities. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h1)

question: Which of the following is a primary objective of a disease surveillance system?

options.B: Early detection of epidemics and health emergencies
options.D: Issuing medical licenses to newly graduated nurses

explanation: The core operational goal of tracking health data is to catch outbreaks early so containment measures can be deployed rapidly. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h2)

question: How do surveillance data directly assist health authorities in resource-limited environments?

options.A: By replacing traditional clinical diagnoses with computer algorithms
options.B: By eliminating the need for community health workers entirely
options.C: By automatically generating pharmaceutical patents for local laboratories
options.D: By providing evidence to justify funding and target interventions effectively

explanation: Hard data proves where the greatest disease burden lies, enabling managers to direct limited supplies and personnel where they are needed most. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h2)

question: What characterizes passive disease surveillance?

options.A: Clinicians routinely report cases to health authorities without prompting
options.B: Laboratory confirmation is legally required before any case is noted
options.C: Public health officers actively visit every village to search for illness
options.D: Data is gathered exclusively from a few selected sentinel hospitals

explanation: Passive surveillance relies on busy health workers remembering to send in regular reports without outside pressure or active searching. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h3)

question: When would public health officials most likely implement syndromic surveillance?

options.A: When they need to audit the financial records of private medical pharmacies
options.B: When they want to calculate the exact annual budget required for surgical equipment
options.C: When early detection of an unusual cluster of symptoms is needed before lab tests confirm a diagnosis
options.D: When routine passive reporting has captured 100 percent of all confirmed cases

explanation: Syndromic surveillance tracks symptom patterns rather than waiting for slow laboratory tests, giving a vital head start during outbreaks. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h3)

question: What is the final operational step in the standard disease surveillance cycle?

options.A: Purchasing new laboratory reagents for tertiary hospitals
options.B: Dissemination of information to decision-makers and stakeholders
options.C: Punishing facilities that fail to report zero cases
options.D: Immediate destruction of raw paper records after data entry

explanation: Data must be shared back out through dissemination reports so that clinicians and leaders can act on the insights gained. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h4)

question: What happens when data analysis and interpretation are skipped in a surveillance system?

options.A: Raw numbers remain uninformative and fail to guide public health action
options.B: Community members immediately stop reporting their symptoms
options.C: The system automatically upgrades to active sentinel surveillance
options.D: Disease outbreaks naturally resolve themselves faster

explanation: Raw case counts without analysis and interpretation are just numbers on a page; they do not reveal trends or justify interventions. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h4)

question: Why are standardized case definitions essential in disease surveillance?

options.A: They ensure uniform reporting standards across different health facilities
options.B: They dictate the exact architectural layout of community health posts
options.C: They replace the need for physical examination by a registered nurse
options.D: They guarantee that patients receive free medications at the pharmacy

explanation: Standard definitions ensure that every healthcare worker counts the same illness the same way, making data comparable across regions. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h5)

question: A community health worker identifies a patient with sudden watery diarrhea during a cholera outbreak season. How should this event be handled under standard reporting mechanisms?

options.A: Held in the clinic logbook until the routine monthly summary report is due
options.B: Reported immediately through emergency channels as a suspected case
options.C: Ignored until laboratory culture results confirm the exact bacterial strain
options.D: Forwarded only to international funding agencies for verification

explanation: Epidemic-prone diseases like cholera require immediate notification as suspected cases to trigger rapid public health containment. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h5)

question: What are the three core epidemiological dimensions used when analyzing surveillance data?
explanation: Descriptive epidemiology relies on analyzing when cases occur, where they happen, and who is getting sick. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h6)

question: What is the primary function of an epidemic curve during an investigation?

options.A: To visualize the time course and pattern of an outbreak
options.B: To schedule nursing shift rosters for emergency wards
options.C: To calculate the total financial cost of hospital admissions
options.D: To audit the attendance records of community volunteers

explanation: An epidemic curve is a graph showing the number of cases over time, helping investigators see if an outbreak is peaking or declining. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h6)

question: Which responsibility is a primary nursing contribution to community surveillance?

options.A: Conducting formal epidemiological research studies for academic journals
options.B: Detecting unusual symptom clusters during daily clinical consultations
options.C: Designing national public health legislation in parliamentary sessions
options.D: Manufacturing vaccines in centralized national laboratories

explanation: Because nurses interact directly with patients daily, they are ideally positioned to spot unusual disease patterns first. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h7)

question: How do nurses strengthen surveillance when participating in immunization campaigns?

options.A: By auditing the financial accounts of the local government health department
options.B: By prescribing broad-spectrum antibiotics to every household visited
options.C: By replacing traditional clinic registers with digital bookkeeping software
options.D: By actively searching for hidden cases and unreported illnesses in the community

explanation: Immunization outreaches bring nurses into homes and remote areas where they can uncover cases that never reached a health facility. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h7)
